rule: Section 3.2.4 — Number serialization per ES6. Integer 0 serializes as "0".
Section 3.2.4 — ES6 JSON.stringify(-0) produces "0" (ToString(-0) === "0"). JCS follows ES6 number serialization.
divergence_trap: An implementation preserving signed zero might output "-0", or an arbitrary-precision library might distinguish -0 from 0.

rule: Section 3.2.4 — Integer values within safe integer range serialize as plain integers without decimal point or exponent.
Section 3.2.4 — Non-integer numbers serialize using ES6 shortest representation. 1.5 is exactly representable and has no shorter form.
Section 3.2.4 — ES6 ToString for numbers ≥ 1e21 uses scientific notation with explicit sign on exponent: 1e+21.
divergence_trap: Implementations using fixed notation for all numbers, or using "1e21" without the + sign, or outputting the full decimal "1000000000000000000000" would diverge.

rule: Section 3.2.4 — ES6 uses scientific notation for non-zero numbers with magnitude < 1e-6. 1e-7 = 0.0000001, which is < 1e-6, so scientific notation is used.
divergence_trap: Implementations using fixed notation might output "0.0000001" instead of "1e-7".

rule: Section 3.2.4 — The ES6 scientific notation threshold is magnitude < 1e-6 (strictly less than). 0.000001 = 1e-6 is NOT less than 1e-6, so decimal notation is used.
divergence_trap: Implementations using a ≤ boundary or different threshold might output "1e-6" instead of "0.000001".

rule: Section 3.2.4 — 2^53 = 9007199254740992 is exactly representable as a double. ES6 serializes it as a plain integer since it is < 1e21.
Section 3.2.4 — 9007199254740993 is beyond 2^53 and not exactly representable as a double. The nearest double is 9007199254740992. After parsing, JSON.stringify serializes this as "9007199254740992".
divergence_trap: An arbitrary-precision JSON parser might preserve "9007199254740993" as a distinct value. A JCS implementation must parse per ES6 double precision.

rule: Section 3.2.2 — The solidus character (U+002F) MUST NOT be escaped. This is a key divergence from many JSON libraries that escape / as \/.
divergence_trap: JavaScript JSON.stringify does NOT escape / by default, but many other implementations (Java Jackson, Go encoding/json, Python json with default settings) DO escape / as \/, producing "http:\/\/example.com".

vector_name: Escaped solidus in input → unescaped in output
rule: Section 3.2.2 — Solidus MUST NOT be escaped in JCS output. The input \/ is parsed as /, and JCS re-serializes as / without escaping.
divergence_trap: Implementations might preserve the input escape style, outputting "http:\/\/example.com" instead of "http://example.com".

rule: Section 3.2.2 — Quotation mark (U+0022) MUST be escaped as \", reverse solidus (U+005C) MUST be escaped as \\.
divergence_trap: Implementations skipping these escapes or using different escape forms would produce invalid JSON or non-compliant JCS.

rule: Section 3.2.2 — Non-BMP characters (above U+FFFF) MUST be serialized as UTF-16 surrogate pairs using \uXXXX escapes. U+1F600 → high surrogate 0xD83D, low surrogate 0xDE00 → \uD83D\uDE00.
divergence_trap: Implementations outputting raw UTF-8 bytes for non-BMP characters (F0 9F 98 80 for 😀) produce valid JSON but are NOT JCS-compliant. The JCS output must be the 12 ASCII bytes of \uD83D\uDE00.

rule: Section 3.2.2 — Control characters (U+0000-U+001F) MUST be escaped. ES6/JSON.stringify uses shorthand escapes where available: U+000A (newline) → \n, U+0009 (tab) → \t, etc. Other control characters use \uXXXX form.
divergence_trap: Implementations using \u000A instead of \n for newline, or failing to escape control characters, would diverge. Some JCS discussions debate whether all control chars must use \uXXXX form exclusively.

rule: Section 3.2.1 — Object keys sorted in ascending order by UTF-16 code unit values. For pure ASCII keys, this is alphabetical/lexicographic order.
divergence_trap: Implementations preserving insertion order, or using locale-aware sorting, produce different key orders.

vector_name: UTF-16 ordering divergence — non-BMP vs BMP ≥ U+E000
rule: Section 3.2.1 — Keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit order. Key1 (U+1F600) UTF-16: [0xD83D, 0xDE00]. Key2 (U+FB00) UTF-16: [0xFB00]. Compare first code unit: 0xD83D (55357) < 0xFB00 (64256), so Key1 sorts first. In Unicode code point order, U+FB00 (64256) < U+1F600 (128512), so Key2 would sort first — DIVERGENCE. In the canonical output, U+FB00 (BMP, not requiring escaping) appears as raw UTF-8 bytes (EF AC 80), not as \uFB00 escape.
divergence_trap: Implementations sorting by Unicode code point order would swap the keys: {"\uFB00":2,"\uD83D\uDE00":1}. This is the most important JCS divergence trap — UTF-16 code unit ordering vs. code point ordering gives DIFFERENT results for any BMP character in U+E000-U+FFFF compared with any non-BMP character.

vector_name: Unicode normalization NON-behavior — NFC vs NFD
rule: Section 3.2.2 and general JCS design — JCS does NOT perform Unicode normalization (NFC, NFD, NFKC, NFKD). The two keys \u00E9 (NFC é, single code point U+00E9) and \u0065\u0301 (NFD é, 'e' + combining acute U+0301) are treated as distinct keys. UTF-16 ordering: [0x0065, 0x0301] vs [0x00E9]; 0x0065 < 0x00E9, so NFD key sorts first. Both keys are BMP and output as raw UTF-8 (é as C3 A9, e as 65, combining acute as CC 81).
divergence_trap: An implementation performing NFC normalization would treat both keys as equivalent (both normalize to U+00E9 é), potentially collapsing to one key or producing undefined behavior. JCS explicitly does NOT normalize — the two keys remain distinct.

rule: Section 3.2.1, 3.2.5 — Empty objects serialize as {}, empty arrays as []. No whitespace is added.

vector_name: Nested structure with key sorting at each level
rule: Section 3.2.1 — Keys sorted at EVERY nesting level. Array elements preserve their order (arrays are NOT sorted).
divergence_trap: Implementations sorting only top-level keys, or sorting array elements, or using unstable sorting, would produce incorrect output.

rule: RFC 8259 Section 4 states: 'When the names within an object are not unique, the behavior of software that receives such an object is unpredictable.' JCS does not explicitly address duplicate keys. Behavior is implementation-defined.
divergence_trap: Some implementations use the first value (output: {"a":1}), some use the last (output: {"a":2}), some reject the input, some preserve both keys. No single correct answer exists.

rule: Section 3.2.4 — ES6 uses scientific notation only for |m| ≥ 1e21 or (m ≠ 0 and |m| < 1e-6). 1e20 is < 1e21, so decimal notation is used. The number 1e20 (10^20) is beyond 2^53 and not exactly representable, but ES6 finds the shortest decimal representation that parses back to the same double.
divergence_trap: Implementations might use scientific notation "1e+20" or output a slightly different decimal due to double rounding. The exact ES6 boundary (1e21) and shortest-representation algorithm must be followed precisely.
